newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary CPI to drop despite March halt - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hungary CPI to drop despite March halt - analysts.

text.p: Hungary's March CPI figures released on Friday are better than expected and inflation is seen dropping in the longer term despite a halt in a 14-month trend of decline in March, analysts said on Friday.
The Central Statistical Office (KSH) said earlier on Friday that the rise in the consumer price index was 18.8 percent in March in year-on-year terms, unchanged from February.
The March figure broke a trend of a consistent drop in the CPI every month since January 1996, when inflation was running at 28.9 percent.
"The majority (of analysts) expected a higher figure for March, due to the effect of January energy price hikes," said Attila Torok of Postabank Securities.
"But the impact of government price hikes was substantial in February already, and the energy price rise was built in the price index," he added.
The forecasts of 14 analysts for March CPI in a recent Reuters survey averaged 19.05 percent.
Analysts said on Friday that they still expected Hungary's inflation to decline by the end of the year, and drop further next year, although they added the government's forecasts were optimistic.
The government targets 17 percent inflation by December this year and said the CPI may go down to around 10 percent in 1998.
Analysts' views about how inflation would run through the year were mixed.
Most analysts said that inflation was likely to drop until at least June, but was likely to stagnate or rise again during the subsequent months, in September at the latest.
They said a rise would be due to the impact of increase in the prices of seasonal goods, for which the price indices were very low, or even negative in the summer of 1996.
"Drops in these prices came as a miracle last year, and a miracle like this usually does not happen twice in the Hungarian economy," said Judit Barta of GKI Research.
Regular quarterly energy price adjustments could also result in monthly rises in inflation, analysts said.
If the government approves the anti-inflationary programme, or reduces the monthly rate of forint devaluation, currently 1.1 percent, it may help inflation to drop, analysts said.

Barta expected the CPI to rise until August, while Torok forecast that inflation would go slightly up from June due to the impact of growing demand spurred by increasing household consumption as well as state and local municipality investments.

He added that relatively low prices in the last quarter of 1996, due to the postponement of energy price hikes originally planned for September 1996, would also contribute to rising year-on-year CPI figures at the end of this year.
All analysts agreed that inflation would decline further in 1998.
Forecasts of analysts in the Reuters survey for year-on-year inflation averaged 18.39 percent for 1997 and 13.35 percent for 1998.
